title: Three Levels of MGCs
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Building on his earlier piece about the "MGC inflection point," Dave Stuart Jr. lays out three progressively deeper levels of Moments of Genuine Connection (MGCs) that teachers can move through across a school year. Level 1 is simply pulling a student aside to ask a question and listen; Level 2 involves delivering a message crafted specifically for one student, illustrated by his brief hallway exchange thanking a student named Draven for bringing him a cookie; Level 3 means addressing something serious — disengagement, declining work quality, falling asleep in class — in a respectful, earnest way, which he demonstrates with sample scripts and a story of pulling struggling students into the hallway with their grades pulled up on his laptop. He supplies prompt questions teachers can use to identify candidates for Level 2 connections by scanning their own roster. Stuart closes by cautioning that Level 3 isn't the goal to constantly chase — the aim is fluency across all three levels, deployed with creativity, enjoyment, earnestness, and amicability as circumstances call for them.
points: Stuart structures MGCs into three deliberately escalating levels — asking a question, delivering a personalized message, and addressing something serious — as a scaffold for teachers new to the practice.
His Level 2 example (thanking a student for a cookie with a specific, personal "Respect, young man") shows how brief and simple a high-impact MGC can be.
For Level 3, he provides verbatim conversational templates for raising concerns about sleeping in class, focus, or declining work quality without accusation.
He explicitly warns against treating Level 3 as the aspirational default, arguing the actual goal is fluency across all three levels rather than constant escalation.
The roster-scanning prompt list gives teachers a concrete method for generating Level 2 MGC ideas rather than waiting for inspiration.
quotes: The most consistently enjoyable and powerful kinds of MGCs are where you have a message to share with just one particular student.
Hey Draven — thank you for bringing that cookie. I really appreciated that. It was kind and thoughtful. Respect, young man.

Sometimes, MGCs are most powerful when we address hard topics with a student. These kinds of conversations indicate that we're paying attention, we're concerned, and we're available to help if they need it.
You're going to be successful someday — I know that. What I want is for you to be successful this year, now.
The one thing I DON'T want you to take away from this article is that we should always be striving for Level 3 MGCs. I don't think that's the goal.
